lessons.title: Linux scheduling - CFS, EEVDF and real-time classes
lessons.summary: How Linux actually picks the next thread - scheduling classes, CFS's virtual runtime and weights, nice values, the EEVDF scheduler that replaced CFS in 6.6, and the SCHED_FIFO, SCHED_RR and SCHED_DEADLINE real-time policies.
lessons.body:
The previous lesson's MLFQ guesses which jobs are interactive and rewards them. Linux took a different route in 2007: stop guessing, and divide the CPU **fairly**, in proportion to a weight. That idea, the Completely Fair Scheduler (CFS), ran almost every Linux machine for 16 years. In 2023 its core was replaced by **EEVDF**, which keeps the fairness and adds an explicit notion of latency.

Real-time work sits above all of this, in strict-priority classes that the fair scheduler never overrides.

## A short history

| Kernel | Scheduler |
|---|---|
| 2.4 | O(n): scan every task |
| 2.6.0 (2003) | O(1): priority arrays plus interactivity heuristics |
| 2.6.23 (2007) | CFS |
| 6.6 (2023) | EEVDF replaces CFS's pick logic |
| 6.12 (2024) | sched_ext: schedulers in BPF |

The O(1) scheduler was fast but relied on heuristics to guess which tasks were interactive, much like MLFQ. Those heuristics could be fooled, and desktop latency suffered under load. Con Kolivas's fairness-based RSDL patches showed a simpler approach worked, and Ingo Molnar wrote CFS in response.

## Scheduling classes

The kernel doesn't have one scheduler; it has a stack of **scheduling classes**, checked in strict order. Ordinary selection considers higher classes first, subject to bandwidth limits. A deadline-class fair server can also dispatch fair work to prevent starvation.

```
stop      (kernel internal, per CPU)
deadline  SCHED_DEADLINE
rt        SCHED_FIFO, SCHED_RR (1-99)
fair      SCHED_NORMAL, SCHED_BATCH,
          SCHED_IDLE
ext       sched_ext (BPF, if loaded)
idle      the idle task
```

Ignoring throttling and fair-server service, an eligible `SCHED_FIFO` thread outranks normal threads regardless of nice. Ordinary applications usually use `SCHED_NORMAL` (`SCHED_OTHER` in the userspace API). A loaded sched_ext scheduler can take over normal, batch and idle-policy tasks; in partial mode it handles only `SCHED_EXT` tasks.

## CFS: an ideal CPU, simulated

CFS's design starts from an imaginary "ideal multi-tasking CPU" that runs all *n* runnable tasks simultaneously, each at 1/*n* speed. Real hardware can run only one task per CPU at a time, so CFS tracks how far each task has fallen behind that ideal.

The tool is **virtual runtime** (`vruntime`), in nanoseconds. When a task runs for a real time *Δ*, its vruntime grows by:

```
vruntime += delta * 1024 / weight
```

The rule for picking is then trivial: **run the task with the smallest vruntime**, the one that has had least.

To find it fast, CFS keeps runnable tasks in a **red-black tree** ordered by vruntime, caching the leftmost node. Picking is O(1); inserting a task after it runs or wakes is O(log *n*).

```
          [B 40]
         /      \
     [A 25]    [D 70]
     /
 [C 10] <- leftmost: runs next
```

As C runs, its vruntime rises and it moves right; eventually another task becomes leftmost and preempts it. A small granularity stops tasks swapping every microsecond and thrashing the cache.

### Weights and nice

Nice values map to weights through a fixed table. Nice 0 is 1024, and each step is a factor of about **1.25**:

| Nice | Weight |
|---|---|
| −20 | 88761 |
| −5 | 3121 |
| 0 | 1024 |
| 1 | 820 |
| 5 | 335 |
| 19 | 15 |

For two otherwise equal competitors in one fair group, moving one from nice 0 to nice 1 changes the split from 50/50 to about 55.5/44.5. The share change depends on the competitors. A higher weight makes vruntime grow *more slowly*, so the task stays leftmost for longer and gets more real CPU.

> [!example] Who gets what?
> Three CPU-bound tasks in the same fair group share one CPU: A and B at nice 0, C at nice 5. Total weight = 1024 + 1024 + 335 = 2383.
> - A: 1024 / 2383 ≈ 43%
> - B: ≈ 43%
> - C: 335 / 2383 ≈ 14%
>
> Check with vruntime: after 10 ms of real time each, A and B gain 10 ms of vruntime, but C gains 10 × 1024 / 335 ≈ 30.6 ms. C becomes "rightmost" three times as fast, so it runs about a third as often.

Note what nice is *not*: it's not a strict priority. A nice 19 task alongside a nice 0 task still gets 15 / 1039, about 1.4%. That proportional share assumes competition within the same fair group, available CPU bandwidth and no overriding higher-class work.

### Sleepers and new tasks

A task that sleeps for a minute would wake with a tiny vruntime and monopolise the CPU while it "caught up". CFS prevents this with `min_vruntime`, a monotonic floor tracking the smallest vruntime in the queue. A waking task's vruntime is raised to roughly `min_vruntime` minus a small bonus (half a latency period), so interactive tasks get a modest head start, not a minute's worth. New tasks start near `min_vruntime` too.

### Latency and slices

CFS had no fixed quantum. It aimed to run every runnable task once within a **target latency** (6 ms by default, scaled by 1 + log2 of the CPU count, capped at 8 CPUs), with a minimum slice of 0.75 ms (also scaled) so that hundreds of tasks wouldn't each get microseconds.

That worked, but latency was a side effect of fairness. There was no way to say "this task wants short, frequent slices", so CFS grew wake-up heuristics to keep desktops snappy, and these were hard to reason about.

## EEVDF: fairness plus deadlines

**Earliest Eligible Virtual Deadline First** comes from a 1995 paper by Ion Stoica and Hussein Abdel-Wahab. Peter Zijlstra's implementation became the fair-class scheduler in Linux 6.6. Weights, nice and the red-black tree stay; the *picking rule* changes.

Two ideas:

1. **Lag.** Compare the service a task should have received on the ideal CPU with what it actually got. Positive lag means it is owed CPU; negative means it has had more than its share. In practice the kernel computes the weighted average vruntime *V* of the queue, and a task is **eligible** if its vruntime ≤ *V* (lag ≥ 0).
2. **Virtual deadline.** Each task requests a slice *r* (by default the base slice). Its deadline is its vruntime plus that slice scaled by weight:

```
deadline = vruntime + r * 1024 / weight
```

The rule: **among eligible tasks, run the one with the earliest virtual deadline.**

Eligibility keeps it fair: nobody who is ahead of their share gets picked. Deadlines add latency control: a task asking for a **shorter slice** gets an earlier deadline, so it runs sooner, though in smaller pieces. Over time it gets the same total share.

> [!example] Short slice, same weight
> A and B are both nice 0 with vruntime 0. A uses a 3 ms slice; B asks for 1 ms.
> - Both are eligible (vruntime 0 = *V*).
> - Deadlines: A = 0 + 3 = 3, B = 0 + 1 = 1.
> - B runs first, for 1 ms. Its vruntime becomes 1 and its next deadline 2.
>
> B now waits for A to catch up before it is eligible again, so neither gets more than its half. B simply gets its half in smaller, more frequent pieces.

In the checked Linux 6.12 source the unscaled base slice is 0.75 ms; the default logarithmic scaling gives 3 ms at eight or more CPUs. Tunables and later kernels can differ. Since Linux 6.12 a normal task can request its own slice, between 0.1 ms and 100 ms, through the `sched_runtime` field of `sched_setattr()`.

Lag also needs care for sleepers. A task that sleeps with negative lag shouldn't erase its debt by sleeping briefly. Current kernels keep such a task on the queue in a "deferred dequeue" state so its lag decays, rather than simply resetting it.

> [!note] Is CFS gone?
> The name lingers: the fair class still lives in `kernel/sched/fair.c`, and many docs and tools still say CFS. Weights, nice, vruntime, group scheduling and CFS bandwidth control all carried over. What changed is how the next task is chosen and how preemption is decided.

## Fairness between whom?

Linux schedules **threads**, not processes. Within one fair group, equal-weight runnable threads compete individually: sixteen such threads collectively receive sixteen shares against one for a single-threaded competitor, when CPU capacity is contested. Two mechanisms rebalance this:

- **Group scheduling**: with cgroups, the fair scheduler first divides CPU between groups (by `cpu.weight` in cgroup v2, default 100), then between tasks within a group. systemd puts each service and user session in its own cgroup.
- **Autogroup** (since 2.6.38): on kernels with it enabled, each terminal session gets its own group, so a `make -j32` in one terminal doesn't swamp your desktop.

One surprise follows: under group scheduling, a thread's nice value only matters **relative to other threads in the same group**. `renice` on a process in one session does nothing against a process in another.

## Real-time classes

For audio, industrial control and low-latency trading, fairness is the wrong goal. The `rt` class gives **strict priorities** from 1 to 99 (higher wins):

- **SCHED_FIFO**: runs until it blocks, yields or is preempted by a higher RT priority. No time slice at all.
- **SCHED_RR**: the same, but threads at *equal* priority rotate with a time slice (100 ms by default, `sched_rr_timeslice_ms`).

```python
import os

# Needs CAP_SYS_NICE or
# sufficient RLIMIT_RTPRIO
os.sched_setscheduler(
    0, os.SCHED_FIFO, os.sched_param(50))
print(os.sched_getscheduler(0)
      == os.SCHED_FIFO)  # True
```

From the shell: `chrt -f 50 ./audio-engine`, and `chrt -p <pid>` to inspect.

> [!warning] A runaway FIFO thread
> A `SCHED_FIFO` thread stuck in a busy loop never yields, so nothing below it runs on that CPU: not your shell, not `kill`. Linux guards against this. RT throttling commonly limits RT work to 950 ms per 1 s (`sched_rt_runtime_us` / `sched_rt_period_us`). Linux 6.12 also introduced a deadline-class fair server that can supply CPU to fair tasks. These are distinct mechanisms; behaviour depends on kernel version, configuration and tunables.

### SCHED_DEADLINE

Since Linux 3.14, the top policy is **SCHED_DEADLINE**. Instead of a priority, a task declares three numbers:

- **runtime**: CPU time needed per period;
- **deadline**: by when, relative to the period start;
- **period**: how often it repeats.

```
chrt -d --sched-runtime  5000000 \
        --sched-deadline 10000000 \
        --sched-period  16666666 0 ./render
```

That says "5 ms of CPU every 16.7 ms frame, finished within 10 ms". The kernel schedules deadline tasks by **Earliest Deadline First**, and uses the Constant Bandwidth Server to stop any task exceeding its runtime. It also performs **admission control**: if the new task's utilisation (runtime / period) would push the total over the permitted limit, `sched_setattr()` fails with `EBUSY`. Admission checks reserve bandwidth; acceptance alone is not a universal proof that application deadlines will be met. Worst-case execution time, blocking, deadline versus period, CPU topology and scheduling assumptions still matter. The kernel documentation distinguishes schedulability tests from the simpler utilization admission test.

### The other fair policies

- **SCHED_BATCH**: fair share, but treated as CPU-bound and preempts others less; good for batch jobs that want cache-friendly long runs.
- **SCHED_IDLE**: extremely low-weight background work in the fair class. It is not the per-CPU idle task and does not promise zero service whenever normal work is runnable.

## Seeing it on a real system

```
$ ps -eLo pid,tid,cls,rtprio,ni,comm
  PID   TID CLS RTPRIO  NI COMMAND
  612   612  TS      -   0 sshd
  880   901  FF     50   - audio-engine
 1200  1200  TS      -  19 backup
```

`TS` is the fair class, `FF` is FIFO, `RR` is round robin, `DLN` is deadline. In `top`, real-time tasks show `rt` in the PR column.

`/proc/<pid>/sched` shows a task's vruntime, slice and switch counts, and `perf sched` records scheduling latency. Scheduler tunables moved from `/proc/sys/kernel` to `/sys/kernel/debug/sched/` in 5.13, a signal that they're for debugging, not routine tuning.

## Pitfalls

- **Expecting nice to be a priority.** It's a weight. Nice 19 gets a small fair share; `SCHED_IDLE` gives background work an even smaller weight, not a strict idle-only guarantee.
- **Renicing across groups.** With autogroup or cgroups, nice only competes within the group. Use `cpu.weight` between groups.
- **Making things real-time "to be safe".** An RT thread that spins starves everything below it, including kernel threads that it may depend on. Use RT for short, bounded work.
- **RT with ordinary locks.** RT threads sharing locks with normal threads invite priority inversion; use `PTHREAD_PRIO_INHERIT` mutexes.

## Key takeaways
- Linux stacks scheduling classes: deadline, then real-time, then fair, then idle. Bandwidth controls and deadline-class fair-server service qualify this ordering.
- CFS gives each task CPU in proportion to its weight by always running the task with the smallest vruntime; vruntime grows more slowly for heavier tasks.
- Nice maps to weights that differ by about 1.25× per step (CPU shares depend on competing weights); it's proportional sharing, not strict priority.
- EEVDF (6.6+) keeps the weights but picks the eligible task (lag ≥ 0) with the earliest virtual deadline, so shorter requested slices mean lower latency without a bigger share.
- SCHED_FIFO and SCHED_RR give strict priorities 1–99; SCHED_DEADLINE reserves runtime using deadline/period parameters and admission control; application deadline guarantees require additional schedulability assumptions. All are powerful enough to starve the system, which is why limits exist.

questions.prompt: On one Linux CPU, X is SCHED_FIFO priority 1 and busy-loops. Y is SCHED_NORMAL at nice −20. Ignoring RT throttling, fair-server service and other tasks, which runs?

options.text: Y, because nice −20 is the highest possible priority
options.explanation: Nice −20 is the heaviest weight *within the fair class*. It doesn't let a normal thread compete with the real-time class at all.

options.text: They share the CPU in proportion to their weights
options.explanation: Proportional sharing only happens within the fair class. Classes are checked in strict order, so there's no sharing between X and Y.

options.text: X, because any runnable real-time thread beats every fair-class thread
options.explanation: Correct. The rt class sits above the fair class. Even RT priority 1 beats nice −20; Y only runs if X blocks (or throttling/the fair server steps in).

options.text: Y, because FIFO priority 1 is the lowest real-time priority and gets demoted
options.explanation: Linux never demotes RT threads into the fair class. Priority 1 is low only relative to other RT threads.

questions.workedExample: X belongs to the real-time class and outranks Y in the fair class. Under the stated exclusions, X remains runnable and Y receives no CPU. On a real system, RT bandwidth limits and fair-server service can change this outcome.

questions.prompt: A CFS run queue holds four runnable tasks with vruntimes A = 25 ms, B = 40 ms, C = 10 ms, D = 70 ms. Which runs next, and why?

options.text: D, because it has run the most and has proved it's important
options.explanation: CFS is about fairness, not rewarding heavy users. The largest vruntime means the task has had the *most* weighted CPU.

options.text: C, because it has the smallest vruntime, so it has had the least weighted CPU
options.explanation: Correct. CFS always runs the leftmost task in the red-black tree, the one with the smallest vruntime.

options.text: B, because it is the root of the red-black tree
options.explanation: The root is just where the tree happens to balance. CFS picks the leftmost node, which it caches.

options.text: A, because it was enqueued first
options.explanation: CFS doesn't use arrival order; it orders tasks by vruntime.

questions.workedExample:
1. CFS's rule: run the task with the **smallest vruntime**.
2. Sort: C (10) < A (25) < B (40) < D (70).
3. C is leftmost, so C runs.

```
        [B 40]
       /      \
   [A 25]    [D 70]
   /
[C 10]  <- leftmost
```

As C runs, its vruntime grows. Once it passes A's (plus a small granularity), A becomes leftmost and preempts it.

questions.prompt: Two CPU-bound tasks compete alone in the same fair group on one CPU: a nice 19 backup and a nice 0 service, with no quota or higher-class interference. What share does the backup receive?

options.text: The backup never runs while the service is busy
options.explanation: That's strict-priority thinking. Nice is a weight, so the backup still gets a small proportional share.

options.text: The backup gets about half the CPU
options.explanation: Half would mean equal weights. Nice 19's weight (15) is far smaller than nice 0's (1024).

options.text: Roughly 1–2% of the CPU
options.explanation: Correct: 15 / (1024 + 15) is about 1.44%. SCHED_IDLE offers still lower-weight background scheduling, not strict idle-only execution.

options.text: The backup is moved into the idle scheduling class
options.explanation: Nice never changes a task's class. The idle class only holds the per-CPU idle task.

questions.workedExample: Nice 0 has weight 1024 and nice 19 has weight 15. The backup share is 15/1039 ≈ 1.44%; the service receives about 98.56%. These are long-run proportions under the stated assumptions. SCHED_IDLE remains in the fair class and does not guarantee execution only when all normal tasks are absent.

questions.prompt: Two CPU-bound tasks share one CPU at nice 0, so each gets 50%. You `renice` one of them to **nice 1** (weight 820). Roughly what shares do they now get?

options.text: 50% / 50%; one nice step is too small to matter
options.explanation: A nice step changes the weight by about 1.25×, which noticeably shifts the split.
Correct: 1024/1844 ≈ 55.5% and 820/1844 ≈ 44.5%, a gap of about 11.1 percentage points. Each share changes about 5.5 points from 50%.

options.text: About 80% / 20%
options.explanation: That would be a weight ratio of 4:1, roughly six nice steps, not one.

options.text: 100% / 0%, because the higher-priority task always runs
options.explanation: That's strict priority. CFS shares in proportion to weight.

questions.workedExample: Within one fair group, weights 1024 and 820 give shares 1024/1844 ≈ 55.53% and 820/1844 ≈ 44.47%. The gap is about 11.06 percentage points. Each share moved about 5.53 percentage points from 50%; this is not a fixed share change for every possible workload.

questions.prompt: A task at **nice 5** (weight 335) runs for **6 ms** of real CPU time. By how much does its vruntime increase?

options.text: 6 ms
options.explanation: That's the increase for a nice 0 task, whose weight is exactly 1024. Lighter tasks' vruntime grows faster.

options.text: About 2 ms
options.explanation: That divides instead of multiplying: it would be the increase for a task *heavier* than nice 0 (weight ≈ 3072).

options.text: About 18.3 ms
options.explanation: Correct. 6 × 1024 / 335 ≈ 18.3 ms. The light task 'ages' about three times as fast in virtual time, so it gets picked about a third as often.

options.text: 335 ms
options.explanation: The weight is a scaling factor, not a time. vruntime = Δ × 1024 / weight.

questions.workedExample:
1. Formula: vruntime += Δ × 1024 / weight.
2. Plug in: 6 × 1024 / 335 = 6144 / 335 ≈ **18.3 ms**.
3. Compare a nice 0 task: 6 × 1024 / 1024 = 6 ms.

Since CFS runs whichever task has the smallest vruntime, the nice 5 task drifts rightwards in the tree ~3× faster and gets roughly a third the CPU of a nice 0 task.

questions.prompt: On one CPU, process P has **16** CPU-bound threads and process Q has **1**. All are nice 0. First they're in the **same** cgroup; then each process is moved into its **own** cgroup with equal `cpu.weight`. What share does Q get in each case?

options.text: About 6% (1/17), then 50%
options.explanation: Correct. Linux schedules threads, so in one group Q gets 1 of 17 equal shares. With separate equal-weight groups, CPU is split 50/50 between groups first.
Process-level fairness only happens when processes are in separate groups. Within one group, each thread is an equal competitor.

options.text: About 6% (1/17) in both cases
options.explanation: Separate groups change the first level of division: groups share by weight before threads share within a group.

options.text: Nearly 0%, then about 6%
options.explanation: Fair scheduling never starves a nice 0 thread. And with equal-weight groups Q gets half, not 1/17.

questions.workedExample:
**Same group**: the fair scheduler sees 17 equal-weight threads.

- Q's share = 1 / 17 ≈ **5.9%**; P gets ≈ 94%.

**Separate groups, equal weight**: CPU is first divided between groups, then within each.

- Group P: 50%, split among 16 threads (≈ 3.1% each).
- Group Q: 50%, all to its one thread.

This is why systemd puts services in their own cgroups and why autogroup exists: so that thread count doesn't decide who gets the CPU.

questions.prompt: Which statements about Linux's `SCHED_FIFO` and `SCHED_RR` are true? Select all that apply.

options.text: Real-time priorities run from 1 to 99, and a higher number wins
options.explanation: Correct. Unlike nice, RT priorities are 'higher is higher'.

options.text: Ignoring throttling and higher scheduling classes, FIFO has no time slice and runs until blocking, yielding or higher RT priority preemption
options.explanation: Correct. FIFO has no time slice at all.

options.text: SCHED_RR threads rotate with a time slice only among threads of the same priority
options.explanation: Correct. A higher-priority RR thread still preempts immediately; the slice (100 ms by default) only matters for ties.

options.text: A SCHED_RR thread that uses its slice drops to the fair class
options.explanation: RR threads are never demoted out of the rt class. They go to the back of the queue for their own priority.

options.text: Any user can set SCHED_FIFO on their own processes
options.explanation: It needs root, CAP_SYS_NICE, or a suitable RLIMIT_RTPRIO, because an RT thread can starve the whole system.

questions.workedExample: Options 1, 2 and 3 are true under the stated exclusions. RT priority is 1–99; FIFO has no quantum; RR rotates equals. RR does not demote into fair scheduling. Option 5 is false: setting FIFO requires CAP_SYS_NICE or suitable RLIMIT_RTPRIO permissions, not merely ownership.

questions.prompt: On a desktop with autogroup enabled, a `make -j32` runs in terminal 1. In terminal 2 you start a video encoder and run `renice -n -10` on it, hoping to give it most of the CPU over the build. It barely makes a difference. Why?

options.text: renice only takes effect after the process restarts
options.explanation: Nice changes apply immediately to running threads.

options.text: Negative nice values are ignored for non-root users
options.explanation: Without sufficient RLIMIT_NICE or privilege, lowering the numeric nice value fails rather than silently succeeding. Assume the requested change succeeds here.

options.text: The encoder is I/O-bound, so CPU weight doesn't matter
options.explanation: The question assumes CPU-bound encoding and build work. Group scheduling explains why changing an individual thread weight may not change the group share.

options.text: Each terminal session is its own group; nice only competes with threads in the same group, so the two groups still split the CPU by group weight
options.explanation: Correct. Under group scheduling, the CPU is shared between the session groups first. Nice only reorders threads inside the encoder's own group.

questions.workedExample:
1. Autogroup puts each session (terminal) in its own task group.
2. The fair scheduler first divides CPU between groups by group weight. The two groups get roughly equal shares.
3. Inside each group, threads share by their nice weights.
4. The encoder is alone in its group, so changing its nice changes its share **within that group**, i.e. not at all relative to the build.

Fix: raise the group's weight instead (`/proc/<pid>/autogroup` accepts a nice value for the whole autogroup, or use cgroup `cpu.weight`).

questions.prompt:
An EEVDF run queue has three nice 0 tasks (equal weight), so the average vruntime is *V* = 10:

| Task | vruntime | slice |
|---|---|---|
| A | 8 | 3 |
| B | 12 | 0.5 |
| C | 10 | 0.5 |

Which task does EEVDF pick? (Classic CFS would have picked A.)

options.text: A, because it has the smallest vruntime
options.explanation: That's CFS's rule. EEVDF picks by earliest virtual deadline among eligible tasks, and A's deadline (11) is later than C's.

options.text: B, because it has the earliest deadline overall
options.explanation: B's deadline (12.5) isn't the earliest, and in any case B is not eligible: its vruntime 12 > V, so it has had more than its share.

options.text: C, because it is eligible (10 ≤ V) and has the earliest virtual deadline (10.5)
options.explanation: Correct. Eligible tasks are A (deadline 11) and C (deadline 10.5). C's short slice gives it the earlier deadline.

options.text: Whichever task woke most recently
options.explanation: Wake-up order isn't the selection criterion. Wake-ups trigger a preemption check, but the pick is by eligibility and deadline.

questions.workedExample:
1. **Eligibility**: vruntime ≤ V (= 10).
   - A: 8 ≤ 10 ✓
   - B: 12 > 10 ✗ (ahead of its share)
   - C: 10 ≤ 10 ✓
2. **Deadlines** (equal weights, so deadline = vruntime + slice):
   - A: 8 + 3 = 11
   - C: 10 + 0.5 = 10.5
3. Earliest eligible deadline: **C**.

C hasn't had less CPU than A, but by asking for short slices it gets served sooner. It will just get its share in smaller pieces, so fairness is preserved.

questions.prompt: A single-CPU system allows deadline tasks up to **95%** of the CPU. Two `SCHED_DEADLINE` tasks already run: 30 ms per 100 ms, and 40 ms per 100 ms. A third asks for **runtime 12 ms, period 40 ms**. What happens?

options.text: It's accepted and all three tasks will occasionally miss deadlines
options.explanation: SCHED_DEADLINE's point is that it doesn't overcommit. It checks before accepting.

options.text: sched_setattr() fails with EBUSY because total utilisation would be 100%, over the 95% limit
options.explanation: Correct. 0.30 + 0.40 + 0.30 = 1.00 > 0.95, so admission control rejects the new task up front.

options.text: It's accepted at a lower real-time priority
options.explanation: Deadline tasks don't have priorities to fall back on. Either the reservation fits or it is refused.

options.text: It's accepted, and the kernel shortens its runtime to fit
options.explanation: The kernel doesn't silently change a task's parameters. It returns an error so the caller can decide.

questions.workedExample: The requested total utilization is 30/100 + 40/100 + 12/40 = 1.00, above the configured 0.95 admission limit, so the request is rejected with EBUSY, assuming otherwise valid parameters and permissions. A request of 10/40 makes utilization 0.95 and passes this bandwidth check. Passing admission does not alone prove all application deadlines will be met.

questions.prompt: On Linux 6.12+, a latency-sensitive nice 0 audio thread uses `sched_setattr()` to request a **1 ms** slice instead of the default (about 3 ms on this machine). A CPU-bound nice 0 thread shares its CPU. Which effects should you expect? Select all that apply.

options.text: The audio thread's virtual deadlines are earlier, so it tends to be picked sooner when it becomes eligible
options.explanation: Correct. deadline = vruntime + slice × 1024 / weight, so a smaller slice gives an earlier deadline.

options.text: The audio thread now gets a larger long-run share of the CPU
options.explanation: Share is set by weight, and both are nice 0. A short slice changes *when* and *in what size pieces* it runs, not how much in total.

options.text: The audio thread runs in smaller pieces, so there may be more context switches
options.explanation: Correct. Shorter slices mean more frequent switching, the usual latency-versus-overhead trade-off.

options.text: The audio thread moves into the real-time class
options.explanation: A custom slice keeps the task in the fair class. Only an RT or deadline policy moves it to a higher class.

questions.workedExample:
Separate the two levers EEVDF gives you:

1. **Weight (nice)** sets the long-run share. Both threads are nice 0, so each gets ~50% when both are busy. A custom slice doesn't change this.
2. **Slice** sets the virtual deadline: deadline = vruntime + slice × 1024 / weight.
   - Audio: vruntime + 1
   - CPU hog: vruntime + 3

So when both are eligible, audio usually has the earlier deadline and is picked first, but it then runs for only ~1 ms before its deadline moves on. Lower latency, more switches, same share. And it stays a `SCHED_NORMAL` task throughout.

lessons.title: Multicore scheduling, affinity, NUMA and containers
lessons.summary: Scheduling across many CPUs - per-CPU run queues, load balancing and cache affinity, pinning with sched_setaffinity and cpusets, NUMA locality, and why CPU limits in containers cause throttling and tail latency.
lessons.body:
Everything so far assumed one CPU. Servers may expose many logical CPUs, arranged in hardware-dependent hierarchies of SMT threads, cores, caches and memory nodes. The scheduler now answers two questions: *which* thread runs next, and *where*. Getting "where" wrong costs cache misses, remote memory accesses, and, inside containers, whole periods of enforced idleness.

## The hardware the scheduler sees

```
Socket / NUMA node 0        node 1
+-----------------------+   +-------
| L3 (shared)           |   | L3 ...
| core0     core1  ...  |   |
| [t0 t1]   [t2 t3]     |   |
| L1/L2     L1/L2       |   |
+--------local DRAM-----+   +-------
```

- **SMT siblings** (hyper-threads) share one core's execution units and L1/L2 caches. Resource contention can make two busy siblings slower than using separate physical cores; the effect depends on the workloads.
- **Cores in one socket** (or one chiplet) share a last-level cache (L3).
- **NUMA nodes** each have their own memory. Reaching another node's memory goes over an interconnect and is slower.

A thread that has been running on a CPU has a **warm cache** there: its working set is in L1, L2 and L3. Move it, and it pays to reload that state. This is **cache affinity**, and it is the central tension of multicore scheduling: keep threads where their data is, but don't leave CPUs idle while work waits elsewhere.

## One queue or many?

OSTEP frames the two basic designs:

| Design | Pros | Cons |
|---|---|---|
| Single shared queue | Simple, balanced by construction | Lock contention, poor affinity |
| Per-CPU queues | Scalable, natural affinity | Load imbalance |

In a simple global-queue design, scheduling decisions contend for one lock and may move tasks between CPUs. The scaling limit and cache cost depend on implementation and workload; a global queue can also incorporate affinity heuristics.

With **per-CPU run queues**, each CPU schedules from its own queue with no shared lock, and threads tend to stay put. The cost is **imbalance**: CPU 0 might have four runnable threads while CPU 1 is idle. The fix is **migration**, moving threads between queues, typically by **work stealing**: an idle or lightly loaded CPU pulls work from a busier one.

Linux has used per-CPU run queues since the O(1) scheduler in 2.6.0. Go's runtime, Java's ForkJoinPool and Tokio use the same per-worker-queue-plus-stealing idea in user space.

## How Linux balances load

Linux describes the topology as nested **scheduling domains**, built at boot:

```
NUMA   : node0 <---------> node1
MC(LLC): [c0 c1 c2 c3]   [c4 c5 c6 c7]
SMT    : [t0 t1] [t2 t3] ...
```

Balancing happens at each level, more often and more eagerly at the bottom, where moving a thread is cheap (siblings share caches), and less often at the top, where it is expensive (crossing NUMA nodes loses cache *and* memory locality).

Three triggers drive it:

1. **Periodic balancing**: from the scheduler tick, each CPU checks whether its domain is imbalanced and pulls tasks if so. Intervals grow with domain level.
2. **Idle balancing**: a CPU that is about to go idle first tries to pull a task from a busier CPU ("newidle" balancing).
3. **Wake-up placement**: when a thread wakes, the kernel chooses a CPU for it. It prefers the previous CPU (warm cache), or an idle CPU sharing the same last-level cache, and considers placing a wakee near its waker.

The balancer also avoids moving a task that ran very recently, treating it as **cache-hot** (the default threshold, `sched_migration_cost`, is 0.5 ms). Balancing considers several signals, including runnable task counts and PELT averages. PELT tracks load, runnable time and running utilization separately; weighted load and CPU utilization are not interchangeable.

> [!note] SMT is treated specially
> Two busy threads on sibling hyper-threads of one core, while another core sits idle, is a bad placement. Linux's balancer prefers spreading busy work across physical cores first, and only then doubling up on siblings.

## CPU affinity: pinning threads

Sometimes you know better than the balancer. **Affinity** restricts which CPUs a thread may run on.

```python
import os

print(os.sched_getaffinity(0))
# {0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7}

os.sched_setaffinity(0, {2, 3})
print(os.sched_getaffinity(0))
# {2, 3}
```

From the shell: `taskset -c 2,3 ./server`, or `taskset -cp <pid>` to inspect. In C, `sched_setaffinity()` or `pthread_setaffinity_np()` per thread. Affinity is inherited across `fork()`.

Layers of control, from soft to hard:

- **Default (soft affinity)**: the scheduler prefers the last CPU but migrates freely.
- **`sched_setaffinity` / `taskset`**: a hard mask per thread.
- **cpuset cgroups** (`cpuset.cpus`, `cpuset.mems`): a mask for a whole group, which processes inside cannot widen. Kubernetes's static CPU manager can give eligible Guaranteed containers with integer CPU requests exclusive logical CPUs. Whole-core allocation additionally depends on policy options such as `full-pcpus-only`.
- **`isolcpus=` / `nohz_full=` boot options**: remove CPUs from general balancing and, with `nohz_full`, stop the scheduler tick when one task runs there. Used for packet processing, HFT and real-time control.

When pinning helps:

- Latency-critical threads that must never share a core (with the rest of the system kept off those CPUs).
- Keeping a thread on the same NUMA node as its memory or NIC interrupts.
- Benchmarks, where migrations add noise.

When it hurts:

- Pinning everything to the same few CPUs while others idle; the balancer can't fix a mask you set.
- Pinning two hot threads to SMT siblings, so they compete for one core.
- Hard-coded CPU numbers that are wrong on the next machine, or inside a container that was given different CPUs.

## NUMA: memory has an address *and* a location

On a multi-socket server, each node's memory is local to its cores. Remote access cost and interconnect bandwidth depend on the machine and workload.

> [!note] Content gap
> No reproducible machine-specific NUMA measurements accompany this lesson, so no universal remote/local latency multiplier is provided. `numactl --hardware` shows the nodes and a distance table (10 means local; remote nodes are larger, commonly around 20).

Linux normally prefers local allocation. For new private anonymous memory, the first write fault commonly allocates a page near the executing CPU. Explicit policies, cpusets, fallback under memory pressure, huge pages and later migration can change placement. That causes a classic bug:

> [!example] The single-threaded initialiser
> A program allocates and zeroes a 64 GiB array in its main thread on node 0, then starts 32 worker threads spread across both nodes. Assume the main thread stays on node 0, local memory is sufficient, writes fault in new pages and no policy or migration changes placement. The pages then start on node 0. Half the workers make every access remotely, and node 0's memory bandwidth is shared by everyone. Fix: initialise each slice from the thread that will use it, or interleave.

Tools and policies:

- `numactl --cpunodebind=0 --membind=0 ./db` runs a process on node 0's CPUs with node 0's memory.
- `numactl --interleave=all` spreads pages round robin across nodes: distributed allocation rather than guaranteed per-thread locality. It can reduce concentration on one node, but does not guarantee removal of all hot spots. Often a good choice for large shared caches, such as a database buffer pool.
- **Automatic NUMA balancing** (since Linux 3.8, `kernel.numa_balancing`): the kernel periodically unmaps pages to sample which node touches them through "hinting faults", then migrates pages towards their users, or tasks towards their memory. It helps long-running, well-partitioned workloads, at the cost of some overhead.
- `numastat -p <pid>` shows where a process's memory actually lives.

The scheduler is NUMA-aware: its top-level domain balances reluctantly across nodes, because moving a thread can turn accesses to its existing memory into remote accesses; cache hits and pages already elsewhere are exceptions.

## Containers: shares versus quotas

Containers use cgroups to control CPU in two very different ways.

| Control | cgroup v2 file | Behaviour |
|---|---|---|
| Weight | `cpu.weight` | Share *under contention* |
| Quota | `cpu.max` | Hard cap, even when idle CPUs exist |

**Weight** (default 100) is proportional sharing between groups, just like nice between threads. If the machine is otherwise idle, a low-weight container can still use every CPU. It's *work-conserving*.

**Quota** is CFS bandwidth control. `cpu.max` holds "quota period" in microseconds; `200000 100000` means 200 ms of CPU time per 100 ms period, i.e. 2 CPUs' worth. Fair-class CPU time is charged across the group. Exhausted local bandwidth allocations cause throttling even with idle CPUs. Ancestor quotas, per-CPU runtime accounting and configured burst credit also affect the exact timeline.

In Kubernetes, a pod's CPU **request** becomes its cgroup weight, and its CPU **limit** becomes its `cpu.max` quota (with the default 100 ms period).

### How throttling wrecks tail latency

> [!example] Two CPUs of quota, eight busy threads
> A container has `cpu.max = 200000 100000` and a server with 8 worker threads, on a 32-core host. In an idealized model, all 8 run simultaneously from the period boundary, with no other contention, overhead, burst credit or carried local runtime.
> - The group consumes 8 CPU-ms per ms of wall time.
> - 200 ms of quota lasts 200 / 8 = **25 ms**.
> - For the remaining **75 ms** of the period, nothing in the container runs.
>
> A request arriving at t = 26 ms waits at least 74 ms for replenishment in this model. If it then immediately receives a CPU for 5 ms, its latency is 79 ms; queueing behind existing work can add more. Average usage is "2 CPUs, within limit", so dashboards look fine.

The symptom is p99 latency far above p50 while CPU usage looks modest. Check `cpu.stat`:

```
nr_periods 36000
nr_throttled 9100
throttled_usec 412000000
```

Here a quarter of periods were throttled. Ways out:

- **Size thread pools to the quota, not the host.** Eight threads chewing through two CPUs' quota in a quarter of the period is worse than two threads using it smoothly.
- **Remove CPU limits** for latency-sensitive services and rely on requests (weights) for fairness. The trade-off is weaker isolation from competing workloads; inherited parent quotas can still throttle the group.
- **Allow bursting**: `cpu.max.burst` (Linux 5.14+) lets a group bank unused quota for short spikes.
- **Use exclusive CPUs** (eligible Guaranteed containers under Kubernetes static CPU management; whole cores require appropriate policy options) when you need both isolation and predictability.

### Runtimes that count the wrong CPUs

Many runtimes size their worker pools from the CPU count, and the CPU count visible inside a container is usually the **host's**:

- Python's `os.cpu_count()` returns the host's logical CPUs. `os.process_cpu_count()` (3.13+) respects the affinity mask, but **not** a `cpu.max` quota.
- Go 1.25 introduced container-aware defaults: logical CPUs, affinity and cgroup CPU bandwidth all participate. Fractional quotas are rounded up, and the default generally stays at least 2 unless CPU count or affinity is lower. Explicit settings and compatibility controls can override this.
- The JVM has been container-aware since JDK 10 (backported to 8u191).

For example, 64 visible logical CPUs, no narrower affinity and no Python CPU-count override can yield a default maximum of 64 processes despite a two-CPU quota. Workers start as jobs are submitted, with behavior depending on Python version and start method. A simple cgroup-v2 quota reader is:

```python
PATH = "/sys/fs/cgroup/cpu.max"

def cpu_quota():
    try:
        with open(PATH) as f:
            quota, period = f.read().split()
    except FileNotFoundError:
        return None  # not cgroup v2
    if quota == "max":
        return None  # no limit
    return int(quota) / int(period)

# "200000 100000" -> 2.0
# Assumes this path is the relevant cgroup.
```

This helper reads one visible cgroup only. It does not discover the process's cgroup or ancestor limits, handle cgroup v1, or combine quota with affinity. An unlimited leaf can still have a constrained ancestor.

## Pitfalls

- **Treating CPU limits as harmless.** A quota caps every period, not the average. Bursty, multi-threaded services get throttled while looking underused.
- **Ignoring SMT.** "16 CPUs" may be 8 cores. Two hot threads on siblings don't double throughput.
- **Over-pinning.** A hard affinity mask disables the balancer's ability to help; it's only better when you've measured.
- **NUMA-blind initialisation.** First touch puts memory where it's first written, not where it's used.
- **Trusting `cpu_count()`** inside containers.

## Key takeaways
- Linux uses per-CPU run queues for scalability and cache affinity, and fixes imbalance by migrating tasks: periodically, when a CPU goes idle, and at wake-up.
- Scheduling domains mirror the hardware (SMT, shared cache, NUMA); balancing is eager where migration is cheap and reluctant across NUMA nodes.
- Affinity (`sched_setaffinity`, `taskset`, cpusets, `isolcpus`) trades the balancer's flexibility for predictability; measure before pinning.
- On NUMA machines, remote memory is slower; first-touch allocation, `numactl` and automatic NUMA balancing decide where pages live.
- `cpu.weight` shares CPU only under contention; `cpu.max` is a hard per-period quota across all threads, and exhausting it early in a period throttles the whole container, hurting tail latency.

questions.prompt: Why does Linux give each CPU its own run queue instead of sharing one global queue?

options.text: A global queue can't support priorities
options.explanation: A single queue can hold priorities perfectly well. The problems are contention and affinity, not expressiveness.

options.text: Per-CPU queues guarantee perfect load balance
options.explanation: It's the opposite: per-CPU queues can become imbalanced, which is why Linux needs migration and load balancing.

options.text: Per-CPU queues avoid a single lock contended by every CPU, and keep threads on the CPU where their cache is warm
options.explanation: Correct. Scalability and cache affinity are the two wins. The cost is imbalance, which the load balancer fixes.

options.text: Each CPU runs a different scheduling algorithm
options.explanation: Every CPU runs the same scheduling classes. Only the queue of tasks differs.

questions.workedExample:
Compare the two designs:

| | Global queue | Per-CPU queues |
|---|---|---|
| Locking | One lock for all CPUs | Mostly local |
| Affinity | Threads hop CPUs | Threads stay put |
| Balance | Automatic | Needs migration |

On a 64-core machine, every scheduling decision taking the same lock would be a severe bottleneck, and threads bouncing between CPUs would keep reloading their caches. So Linux uses per-CPU queues and pays for it with a load balancer.

questions.prompt:
On an 8-CPU Linux machine with no restrictions, what does this print?

```python
import os
os.sched_setaffinity(0, {1, 5})
os.sched_setaffinity(0, {5, 6})
print(sorted(os.sched_getaffinity(0)))
```

options.explanation: That would be the intersection of the two masks. Each call *replaces* the mask; it doesn't intersect with the previous one.
That would be the union. sched_setaffinity sets a new mask rather than adding to the old one.
The calls do take effect (pid 0 means the calling thread), so the mask is no longer all CPUs.
Correct. The second call replaces the mask with {5, 6}.

questions.workedExample:
1. `sched_setaffinity(0, mask)` sets the calling thread's allowed CPUs to exactly `mask`.
2. First call: {1, 5}.
3. Second call replaces it: {5, 6}.
4. `sched_getaffinity(0)` returns {5, 6}; sorted → `[5, 6]`.

The kernel will now only run this thread on CPUs 5 and 6, and children created with `fork()` inherit that mask.

questions.prompt: A fair-class batch container has cpu.weight=10, no leaf or ancestor quota, access to all 16 physical cores, and enough runnable workers. With no competing work, how much CPU can it use?

options.text: All 16 cores
options.explanation: Correct. Weight only matters under contention. With no competitors, the low-weight group gets everything: weights are work-conserving.

options.text: About 10% of one core
options.explanation: That treats weight as a hard cap. Caps come from cpu.max; weight is a relative share.

options.text: About 1.6 cores (10% of 16)
options.explanation: Again a cap interpretation. Weight 10 means 'a tenth as much as a weight-100 group when both want CPU', not 10% of the machine.

options.text: None until a weight-100 group gives up the CPU
options.explanation: There are no other groups, and weights never stop a group from using idle CPUs.

questions.workedExample:
1. `cpu.weight` is proportional sharing between groups that are **competing**.
2. Here no other group wants CPU, so its share of the contended CPU is 10 / 10 = 100%.
3. With 16 cores and enough threads, it can use all 16.

If a weight-100 group then became busy, the split would be 10 : 100, about 9% vs 91%. A hard ceiling would need `cpu.max`.

questions.prompt: In an idealized quota model, a container has cpu.max = 300000 100000. Ten threads run continuously on ten CPUs from each period boundary, without contention, overhead, burst credit or carried runtime. How long is the group throttled in each 100 ms period?

options.text: 0 ms; 3 CPUs of quota is plenty on a 32-core host
options.explanation: The quota is shared by all threads across all CPUs. Ten busy threads burn through it faster than three would.

options.text: 70 ms
options.explanation: Correct. 10 threads consume 10 CPU-ms per ms, so 300 ms of quota lasts 30 ms. The remaining 70 ms is throttled.

options.text: 30 ms
options.explanation: That's how long the container *runs* before the quota is exhausted, not how long it is throttled.

options.text: 97 ms
options.explanation: That assumes each thread is limited to 0.3 ms. The quota is a pooled budget, not a per-thread one.

questions.workedExample:
1. Quota: 300 ms of CPU per 100 ms period (3 CPUs' worth).
2. Consumption: 10 threads × 1 CPU-ms per ms = 10 CPU-ms per ms.
3. Quota lasts 300 / 10 = **30 ms**.
4. Throttled for 100 − 30 = **70 ms** of the period.

Average use is 3 CPUs, exactly the limit, so a dashboard looks healthy. But any request arriving during those 70 ms waits until the period ends. That's the tail-latency trap.

questions.prompt: A main thread pinned to NUMA node 0 writes every page of a new private 100 GiB array, with enough local memory and no explicit policy or migration. Workers then run on both nodes and bandwidth falls below expectations. Which placement problem fits this setup?

options.text: The workers are being throttled by a cgroup quota
options.explanation: Nothing in the scenario mentions a CPU limit. The clue is who touched the memory first.

options.text: The array is too large for the L3 cache
options.explanation: True of any 100 GiB array, but it doesn't explain why this layout is slow compared with alternatives.

options.text: Linux allocates huge arrays across both nodes evenly by default
options.explanation: The default is first touch, not interleaving. That's exactly why the layout is lopsided.

options.text: First-touch placed every page on the main thread's node, so the other socket's workers make every access remotely and one node's memory bandwidth is shared by all
options.explanation: Correct. Initialise each slice from the thread that will use it, interleave with numactl, or let automatic NUMA balancing migrate pages over time.

questions.workedExample: Under the stated assumptions, first-write faults allocate the new pages on node 0. Workers on node 1 then need remote memory for cache misses to those pages, and requests concentrate on node 0. The exact cost is hardware-dependent; no measured multiplier is available here. Parallel initialization, deliberate interleaving or matching workers to memory can improve placement, subject to measurement.

questions.prompt: On Linux Python 3.13+, with 64 visible logical CPUs, no CPU-count override or affinity restriction, a pod has a two-CPU quota. A default ProcessPoolExecutor is given enough CPU-bound jobs to fill it. What problem can occur?

options.text: It starts 2 workers, because Python reads the cgroup quota
options.explanation: `os.cpu_count()` (and `process_cpu_count()`) don't read cpu.max. Python doesn't see the quota.

options.text: Up to 64 workers compete for two CPUs of aggregate quota, risking heavy throttling
options.explanation: Correct. The default maximum uses process_cpu_count(), which considers affinity but not CPU bandwidth quota. Running many CPU-bound workers can exhaust each period budget early.

options.text: It starts 64 workers, and the limit stops being enforced because there are more processes than CPUs
options.explanation: The quota applies to all processes in the cgroup, however many there are.

options.text: It fails to start because 64 exceeds the limit
options.explanation: Nothing checks pool size against the quota. The workers start; they just can't all run.

questions.workedExample: With the specified environment, process_cpu_count() returns 64, so the default maximum is 64 workers. Their CPU time shares the two-CPU quota. Enough runnable workers may exhaust the budget early and then wait for replenishment. Benchmark a smaller pool; discover effective affinity and cgroup hierarchy limits rather than assuming the host count is usable bandwidth.

questions.prompt: A latency-sensitive service in a container shows p99 far above p50 and `nr_throttled` rising fast, while average CPU is below its limit. Which changes are likely to help? Select all that apply.

options.text: Shrink the worker pool to roughly the CPU quota
options.explanation: Correct. Fewer threads consume the quota more smoothly, so it lasts the whole period instead of being exhausted early.

options.text: Remove the CPU limit and rely on the CPU request (weight) for fairness
options.explanation: Correct, if no ancestor quota remains: removing the limiting bandwidth cap can remove this cause of throttling. Fairness then depends on competing weights and available CPUs.

options.text: Allow bursting with cpu.max.burst
options.explanation: Correct. Banking unused quota lets short spikes run without being throttled, while still bounding average use.

options.text: Raise the pod's cpu.weight (CPU request) but keep the same limit
options.explanation: Weight affects sharing under contention, not the hard per-period quota. Throttling continues unchanged.

options.text: Add more worker threads so requests don't queue
options.explanation: More threads burn the quota faster and make throttling worse.

questions.workedExample: A smaller CPU-bound pool can consume budget more smoothly; removing all relevant quota caps avoids quota throttling; accumulated burst credit can absorb short spikes. Raising weight does not raise the quota. More workers can exhaust it earlier. These are workload-dependent remedies: compare throughput and latency, and inspect ancestor limits.

questions.prompt: A container's `cpu.stat` over the last hour shows `nr_periods 36000` and `nr_throttled 14400`, with the default 100 ms period. What does this tell you?

options.text: The container was throttled for 14,400 seconds
options.explanation: nr_throttled counts periods in which throttling happened, not seconds. The time is in throttled_usec.

options.text: Throttling was reported for 40% of the counted periods; request latency needs separate measurement
options.explanation: Correct. 14400 / 36000 = 0.4. Two periods in five ended with the group out of quota.

options.text: It used 40% of its quota on average
options.explanation: nr_throttled doesn't measure average usage. A group can be throttled often while averaging well under its quota.

options.text: Nothing; nr_throttled only counts throttling of real-time tasks
options.explanation: These cpu.stat fields come from CFS bandwidth control, which applies to normal tasks.

questions.workedExample: 14400 / 36000 = 40%. With continuously active 100 ms enforcement periods, 36000 periods correspond to one hour. These counters alone do not measure request latency or the fraction of wall time stalled. Compare interval deltas, throttled_usec, usage and latency measurements; throttled time can aggregate across per-CPU run queues.

questions.prompt: In an idealized quota model, cpu.max = 50000 100000. One request needs 80 ms CPU and starts at a period boundary. Assume no other work, contention, overhead, burst credit or carried runtime. Roughly when does it finish?

options.text: At 80 ms
options.explanation: That ignores the quota. Only 50 ms of CPU is allowed per 100 ms period.

options.text: At 160 ms
options.explanation: That spreads the work evenly at half speed. Bandwidth control doesn't slow a thread down; it lets it run at full speed, then stops it.

options.text: At about 130 ms
options.explanation: Correct. It runs 0–50 ms, is throttled 50–100 ms, then runs its remaining 30 ms from 100 to 130 ms.

options.text: At 200 ms
options.explanation: The second period doesn't need to be used in full; the request finishes 30 ms into it.

questions.workedExample:
Walk the periods:

```
0    50   100  130
|run |thr |run|
 50ms  -    30ms
```

1. Period 1 (0–100): runs 50 ms, quota gone at 50, throttled until 100.
2. Period 2 (100–200): needs 30 more ms; runs 100–130 and finishes.

So 80 ms of CPU takes ~130 ms of wall time. A request arriving just after the quota ran out would fare worse: it would wait up to 50 ms before starting.

questions.prompt: A machine has 4 physical cores with 2 hyper-threads each (CPUs 0–7, where 0/1, 2/3, 4/5 and 6/7 are siblings). You pin two CPU-bound, cache-heavy threads with `taskset -c 0,1`. The rest of the machine is idle. Compared with letting the scheduler place them, what do you expect?

options.text: Same throughput, since each thread has its own logical CPU
options.explanation: Logical CPUs 0 and 1 share one physical core's execution units and L1/L2, so each thread runs slower than on its own core.

options.text: Better throughput, because the threads share an L1 cache
options.explanation: Sharing helps only if they share data. Two cache-heavy threads with separate data mostly evict each other.

options.text: The scheduler will move one thread to another core to fix the imbalance
options.explanation: A hard affinity mask is never overridden by the load balancer. It can only choose within CPUs 0 and 1.

options.text: Lower throughput: both threads compete for one physical core, while unpinned the balancer would have spread them across cores
options.explanation: Correct. Linux's balancer prefers spreading busy tasks across physical cores before doubling up on SMT siblings. The pin overrode that.

questions.workedExample:
1. CPUs 0 and 1 are **SMT siblings**: one core, shared execution units and L1/L2.
2. Two CPU-bound threads there each get only part of that core.
3. Unpinned, the balancer would see 3 idle physical cores and spread the threads onto separate cores.
4. The affinity mask forbids that, so the kernel can't fix it.

Lesson: if you pin, pin to **different cores** (e.g. `taskset -c 0,2`), and know your topology (`lscpu -e`).

questions.prompt: Which statements about Linux's multicore load balancing are true? Select all that apply.

options.text: A CPU that is about to go idle tries to pull work from a busier CPU first
options.explanation: Correct. This is 'newidle' balancing, one of the three triggers alongside periodic and wake-up balancing.

options.text: Balancing across NUMA nodes is done as eagerly as between SMT siblings
options.explanation: It's the reverse. Moving between siblings is cheap (shared caches), so it happens readily; crossing NUMA nodes loses cache and memory locality, so it's done reluctantly.

options.text: When a thread wakes, the kernel prefers its previous CPU or an idle CPU sharing the same last-level cache
options.explanation: Correct. Wake-up placement balances keeping a warm cache against finding an idle CPU quickly.

options.text: A task that ran very recently may be treated as cache-hot and left where it is
options.explanation: Correct. Below the migration-cost threshold (0.5 ms by default) the balancer prefers not to move it.

options.text: Load is measured purely as the number of runnable tasks on each CPU
options.explanation: Linux considers runnable counts alongside PELT load, runnable and utilization averages, CPU capacity and other signals. It does not rely purely on task counts.

questions.workedExample: The correct statements are 1, 3 and 4. Newidle balancing may pull work; wake-up placement considers locality and idle CPUs; recently running tasks may be treated as cache-hot. Cross-node balancing has different costs. Linux uses multiple signals, including task counts and distinct PELT averages; no one metric describes every balancing decision.
